title: What holds a cell up, and what makes it climb

objectives.statement: Given a stated mechanical demand and the length over which it acts, predict which of the three cytoskeletal filament systems can meet it by comparing persistence length against that length, by testing whether the demand requires a direction, and by testing whether it requires survival under large deformation, and name the property that decided the case.

Place the four attachment structures of a colonic absorptive cell in apical-to-basal order, name the cytoskeletal polymer each one anchors and the proteins that make the link, and use that map to predict which functions survive and which fail when a named component is lost.

Weigh the evidence for and against proliferation in the crypt being the force that drives cells upward, state for each study what its design can and cannot establish about that force, and name the measurement that would discriminate between the competing accounts.

scenes.title: A finger of fluid, standing up
scenes.contentHtml:
A finger of fluid, standing up

Lesson 04 left a puzzle on the table and named this lesson as the place to solve it.

The apical face of a colonic absorptive cell is thrown into thousands of fine projections. Each one is about a micrometre long and about a hundred nanometres across, and together they raise the cell's apical surface area roughly thirtyfold. That much you already have. Here is what lesson 04 could not explain with membranes alone.

The membrane wrapped around one of those projections is two lipid molecules thick, about 5 nanometres, and it behaves as a liquid in its own plane. A lipid in it swaps places with a neighbour millions of times a second. Now try to build a standing cylinder out of that material, twenty times taller than it is wide, and keep it standing while digestive enzymes and bile salts wash past it. Soap film does not do this. A liquid surface pulls itself into the shape with the least area it can reach, which is the opposite of a finger.

So the shape is not coming from the membrane. Something inside is holding it.

What is inside a microvillus

Cut one across and you find a bundle of actin filaments running its full length. Roughly 19 of them, cross-linked into a rod stiff enough to hold the membrane out against surface tension. The bundle continues down past the base of the projection into the cell, where a layer called the terminal web cross-links neighbouring bundles to each other through a non-erythrocytic spectrin. Each bundle is anchored at the bottom into a shared mat, and the mat is what stops nineteen filaments from simply tipping over.

The bundle does not float free inside the tube. Cross-bridges made of myosin-1A with calmodulin reach out sideways from the outer filaments of the bundle to the membrane itself, two or three from each outer filament. The membrane is held on the frame, at intervals, all the way up.

Three proteins do the cross-linking inside the bundle, and they are not interchangeable. Fimbrin is the main one; a bundle assembled with fimbrin alone is indistinguishable from an intact microvillar core. Villin is a secondary cross-linker that makes looser and less regular bundles, and it has a second setting: when calcium rises, villin stops bundling actin and starts severing it. Small espin is present at about a twentieth of the concentration of the others.

Read that villin fact twice, because it is a real design feature. One protein in the core is a switch that can take the core apart.

The end that faces the lumen

The filaments in the bundle all point the same way. Every one is unipolar, with its barbed end, the plus end, embedded in a dense plaque at the very tip of the projection, and its pointed end directed down into the cell. New actin subunits are added exclusively at the barbed end, which is the end at the tip.

That places the growing end of every filament in the bundle at the surface facing the gut contents.

Consider what follows. The part of this structure that is being actively extended is the part pressed against the lumen, the least protected position the cell has. A structure that grows from its exposed tip has to keep supplying subunits to that tip, and it can be shortened from there too. The alternative arrangement, growth from the base, would have let the cell build the projection from safety and push it outward. Actin does not offer that option here, because the filament's own chemistry fixes which end grows.

The projections sit in a regular hexagonal array, 115 to 120 nanometres from centre to centre. They are not a random fringe. They are a packed, spaced, individually guyed set of rods, each one built from a polymer whose direction of assembly the cell does not choose.

Check
id check-why-not-membrane

Before going on, answer in one sentence: why can a lipid bilayer not hold a microvillus in shape by itself?

Then answer a second: if you wanted to shorten every microvillus on a cell quickly, which single protein named above would you go after, and what would you do to it?

The rest of the lesson generalises this. A cell bounded by a fluid gets its shape, its attachments, and its movement from a set of polymers inside it. There are three of them, they have genuinely different mechanics, and the next scene is about why the differences matter more than the names.

scenes.title: Three polymers, and what each one's stiffness will let it do
scenes.contentHtml:
Three polymers, and what each one's stiffness will let it do

Textbooks introduce the cytoskeleton as a list of three: actin filaments, microtubules, intermediate filaments. Memorising the list buys almost nothing. What each one can do for a cell follows from three measurable properties, and once you have those, most of the jobs assign themselves.

The three properties are how stiff a single filament is, whether the filament has a direction, and how far it can be stretched before it fails.

How stiff, expressed as a length

Stiffness for a thin filament is usually quoted as a persistence length: the distance along the filament over which it stays roughly straight against the random kicks of the surrounding water. Below that distance the filament behaves like a rod. Far above it, the filament behaves like cooked spaghetti.

Filament Persistence length Same figure, in micrometres
Microtubule greater than 1 mm greater than 1000 µm
Actin filament 3 to 17 µm 3 to 17 µm
Intermediate filament a few hundred nm to about 1 µm about 0.2 to 1 µm

Three orders of magnitude separate the top row from the bottom. That is not a detail of degree.

Now put a cell next to those numbers. A colonic absorptive cell is about 20 to 25 µm tall. A microvillus on its apical face is about 1 µm long. Those are the two lengths that matter, and the table above is only useful once you compare it against them. The next scene does that comparison properly, as a worked calculation. For now, hold the shape of the answer: a microtubule is rigid across anything cell-sized, an actin filament is stiff over a micrometre and floppy over a cell, and a single intermediate filament is floppy over both.

Whether the filament has a direction

Actin filaments and microtubules are polar. The two ends differ chemically, subunits are added preferentially at one of them, and, decisively, motor proteins can tell the ends apart. Myosins walk on actin. Kinesins and dyneins walk on microtubules. Each motor moves toward a particular end, so a polar filament is a track with a direction on it.

Intermediate filaments are built differently. Their dimers associate in an antiparallel fashion into tetramers that have no net direction, and filaments assembled from those tetramers are apolar. The consequence is not subtle: intermediate filaments carry no molecular motors at all. There is no myosin, kinesin or dynein equivalent for them.

Say what that rules out. Nothing can be carried along an intermediate filament to a chosen destination. No intermediate filament can be walked along to generate directed movement. Whatever intermediate filaments are for, it is not transport and it is not motion.

This is the single most useful distinction in the three-way comparison, and it is the one a list of names hides.

How far it stretches before it fails

Here the ranking inverts, and the floppiest filament turns out to be the toughest.

Intermediate filaments bear far larger extensional strain than microtubules or actin filaments. Several kinds have been stretched past 200 per cent of their resting length without breaking; single filaments reach about 250 per cent, and desmin filaments up to about 350 per cent. Stretching one to three and a half times its length and finding it intact is not behaviour actin or tubulin offers.

Networks of them behave in a related way. A vimentin network's shear modulus climbs by more than an order of magnitude between 1 per cent and 80 per cent strain: the more you deform it, the harder it pushes back. Intermediate filament networks begin to stiffen at around 10 to 20 per cent strain, while actin networks stiffen at strains of a few per cent. Actin resists early and gives way sooner. Intermediate filaments yield early, then refuse to break. Compared directly against actin, intermediate filaments stretch to multiple times their original length and hold force at higher tensile loads.

Putting the three properties together

The argument now closes.

A microtubule is effectively a rigid rod on the scale of a cell, and it is polar. Both properties point the same way: use it to define an axis and to run directed traffic along that axis. In an absorptive intestinal cell, microtubules are in fact arranged along the apical-to-basal axis, which is the axis the cell's whole division of labour is organised around.

An actin filament is stiff over about a micrometre and carries myosin motors. Both properties again point one way: use it to build and to move things the size of a surface projection. That is what the previous scene described, nineteen filaments cross-linked into a beam a micrometre long with myosin cross-bridges holding a membrane onto it.

An intermediate filament is floppy, apolar, motorless, and nearly unbreakable under stretch. It cannot define an axis and it cannot carry anything. What it can do is absorb a large deformation and still be there afterwards. So it is the one to reach for when the question is not "what shape should this be" or "how do I move this", but "how does this tissue survive being pulled about".

A sheet of cells climbing out of a crypt while bacteria and digesta scrape past it is being pulled about constantly. The next question is where in that sheet each of these polymers is anchored, and that is what a junction turns out to be.

scenes.title: Choosing a polymer for a stated job
scenes.contentHtml:
Choosing a polymer for a stated job

The previous scene gave three persistence lengths and two cell dimensions. This scene turns them into a decision procedure you can run on a new structure, and then runs it four times.

The whole method is one comparison. Take the length of the structure that has to be held rigid, call it LL, and divide the filament's persistence length by it.

Read the answer like this. When RR is comfortably greater than 1, the filament stays essentially straight over that distance and behaves as a rod. When RR is about 1 or less, thermal motion bends it appreciably over that distance and a single filament will not hold the shape on its own.

The two lengths in play for a colonic absorptive cell are its height, about 20 to 25 µm, and the length of one microvillus on its apical surface, about 1 µm.

Worked Example
id worked-example-which-polymer

The task. For each of four demands on this cell, decide which filament system can meet it, and say which property decided it.

Demand 1: hold a 1 µm projection out against the surface tension of a fluid membrane.

Start with actin, taking the working figure of about 10 µm for its persistence length.

R=10 μm/1 μm=10R = 10\ \mu\text{m} / 1\ \mu\text{m} = 10

Ten is comfortably above 1, so a single actin filament is rod-like over the length of a microvillus. Check the pessimistic end of the published range as well, because a conclusion that only survives the favourable number is not a conclusion: at the bottom of the 3 to 17 µm range, R=3R = 3, still above 1. The answer holds across the range.

Test an intermediate filament against the same demand. With a persistence length of about 0.2 to 1 µm, RR runs from 0.2 to 1. At best it is marginal, and at worst the filament bends five times over within the length it is meant to hold straight. Intermediate filaments are ruled out here on stiffness alone, without needing any other argument.

A microtubule would certainly be stiff enough, with RR greater than 1000. It is ruled out on a different ground: at about 25 nm across it is a quarter of the width of the projection it would have to sit inside, and the observed structure is a bundle of thin filaments and not one thick tube. Being sufficient is not the same as being what is used.

Answer: actin. Decided by stiffness at the micrometre scale.

Demand 2: define the cell's apical-to-basal axis across its full 20 to 25 µm height.

Actin first, because it won the previous round and a good procedure does not assume the previous answer transfers.

R=10 μm/22 μm≈0.45R = 10\ \mu\text{m} / 22\ \mu\text{m} \approx 0.45

Below 1. A single actin filament is floppy over the height of this cell, so it cannot by itself mark out an axis from apical surface to basement membrane.

Microtubule:

R>1000 μm/25 μm=40R > 1000\ \mu\text{m} / 25\ \mu\text{m} = 40

Forty cell-heights of straightness. A microtubule crossing this cell is, for practical purposes, a straight rod. Add polarity, which gives the axis a direction and lets kinesins and dyneins run traffic one way or the other along it, and the case is made twice over. The observation that microtubules in these cells are in fact arranged along the apicobasal axis agrees with the prediction.

Answer: microtubules. Decided by stiffness at the cell scale, and confirmed by polarity.

Demand 3: carry a vesicle from the Golgi to a chosen face of the cell.

Stiffness is not the deciding property here; direction is. The demand contains the word "chosen", and only a polar filament can distinguish one destination from the other. Actin and microtubules are both polar and both carry motors, so both are admissible, and over a 20 µm journey the microtubule's rigidity and directionality make it the long-haul option.

Intermediate filaments are excluded absolutely, not marginally. They are apolar and carry no motors, so there is no mechanism by which anything could be moved along one in a selected direction. This is a different kind of exclusion from Demand 1: there, intermediate filaments were too floppy for the job, and here, no amount of stiffness would help.

Answer: microtubules, with actin admissible for short distances. Decided by polarity.

Demand 4: keep the sheet intact while it is stretched and scraped for days on end.

Run the stiffness comparison and it gives the wrong kind of answer. Intermediate filaments lose that comparison at every length scale in this cell. So the comparison is the wrong one, which is itself the lesson: pick the property the demand names.

The demand names deformation and survival, so compare extensibility. Intermediate filaments stretch past 200 per cent of their resting length without breaking, some to 350 per cent, and their networks stiffen progressively from about 10 to 20 per cent strain instead of failing. Against actin directly, they hold force at higher tensile loads. Nothing in the actin or microtubule data comes near this.

Their disadvantages are irrelevant to this demand. Floppiness does not matter when the job is to be pulled, not to push. Having no motors does not matter when nothing needs to be transported.

Answer: intermediate filaments. Decided by extensibility, and their apolarity costs nothing here.

What the procedure does not settle

Two limits, and both matter.

The persistence lengths above were measured on purified single filaments in vitro. A cell does not use single filaments; it cross-links them. Nineteen actin filaments tied together into a bundle resist bending far better than one does, so the single-filament figure is a floor on what an actin structure can achieve, not a ceiling. Demand 1 came out the same either way, which is why the argument was safe to make there. Do not carry that luck into a case where the single-filament number lands near R=1R = 1.

And a favourable ratio never establishes that a cell actually uses a given polymer for a given job. Demand 2 was checked against an observation, not left as a prediction. Where an argument from mechanics is all you have, that is where the argument stops.

scenes.title: Four attachments, and which polymer each one grips
scenes.contentHtml:
Four attachments, and which polymer each one grips

Lesson 04 drew the tight junction as a line between two membranes and said plainly that lesson 07 would have to say what the line is made of. Here it is, and there turn out to be four attachments instead of one.

They are not four copies of the same idea. They sit at different heights on the cell, they are built from different proteins, they grip different polymers, and they fail differently. Get the pairing of junction to polymer right and you can predict which of them a given defect implicates. Get it backwards and you cannot.

Down the side of the cell, in order

In a simple epithelium like this one, the tight junction sits most apically. Below it comes the adherens junction with its associated belt of actin, and below that the desmosomes.

The tight junction is the seal. At the tight junction the space between the two cells disappears altogether; at the adherens junction and at the desmosome the neighbouring membranes stay 15 to 20 nanometres apart. That single geometric fact tells you which of the three closes the route between cells and which two do not. Adhesion and sealing are separate jobs, and only the top one of the three does the sealing. It is the rate-limiting step for anything travelling between cells instead of through them.

Its transmembrane proteins are the claudins, occludin, and JAM-A. On the inside, scaffold proteins ZO-1, ZO-2 and ZO-3 connect those to actin. The claudins are what make the seal selective: they form charge-selective pores, so the tight junction is a regulated gate and not a plug.

The tight junction also does a second job that lesson 04 established and this lesson takes as given. Besides sealing the route between cells, it acts as a fence within the plane of the membrane itself, stopping apical membrane components from drifting round into the basolateral face. The original demonstration, in a polarised dog kidney monolayer, found the tight junction blocked diffusion of a fluorescent phospholipid in the outer leaflet and not in the cytoplasmic one. So one structure holds two separations at right angles to each other: it closes the gap between two cells, and it divides one cell's own membrane into two domains. The seal is what the rest of this scene compares against the other attachments; the fence is why the apical and basolateral surfaces you already know about stay different.

The adherens junction below it uses E-cadherin and nectin reaching across to the neighbour, with catenins on the cytoplasmic side connected directly to actin. Its business is starting and stabilising the contact between two cells.

Then the desmosome, and this is where the polymer changes.

The one that does not use actin

A desmosome is built from three classes of protein. Desmosomal cadherins, the desmogleins and desmocollins, reach across the gap to the neighbouring cell. Armadillo proteins, plakoglobin and the plakophilins, sit on the cytoplasmic face. And desmoplakin, a cytolinker, anchors keratin-containing intermediate filaments to the membrane.

So the desmosome grips keratin, and keratin is an intermediate filament.

Now recall what the mechanics said about intermediate filaments. They stretch to multiple times their length without breaking and they hold force at higher tensile loads than actin does. The junction whose job is mechanical coupling under load is precisely the junction wired to the polymer that survives load. The pairing is not arbitrary.

This is the place learners most often invert, so state it in both directions. Adherens junctions link to actin. Desmosomes link to intermediate filaments. If you find yourself saying that desmosomes are the actin ones, you have swapped them, and every downstream prediction will be wrong.

The fourth attachment faces down, not sideways

The three above all join one cell to another. The cell also has to stay attached to what it is sitting on.

Beneath the sheet lies the basement membrane, a mat of laminins, fibronectin and other matrix material. Epithelial cells in the human intestinal crypt bind it through integrins: laminin receptors including the α2β1, α3β1 and α6β4 combinations, and the fibronectin-binding α5β1 among the ones recognising the RGD motif. On the inside, integrin-linked kinase creates a physical link between the integrin β1 tail and actin.

So the basal attachment is an actin-linked one too, and three of the four attachments on this cell converge on the same polymer.

That convergence is worth pausing on. Actin is not the strongest of the three under stretch, and the scene before this one showed intermediate filaments beating it on tensile load. Yet actin gets three of the four attachments. Actin's advantage is that it is polar and carries myosin motors, so an actin-linked attachment can be pulled on, tightened, and released under the cell's control. A keratin-linked attachment can hold, and that is all it can do. The cell distributes its attachments between a polymer it can actuate and a polymer that will not tear.

Two things this scene leaves out

Gap junctions are absent from the map above on purpose. The organising question here is which cytoskeletal polymer an attachment anchors, and this lesson neither asks nor answers what a gap junction does; lesson 06 of this block, on signalling between cells, is the place that question belongs.

Hemidesmosomes are a harder omission and an honest one. The desmosome review used above names hemidesmosomes alongside integrin-based focal adhesions as the structures through which cell-to-matrix adhesion happens, and says no more about them. The crypt study used above describes focal adhesions and integrin-linked kinase in human intestinal crypt cells and does not address hemidesmosomes at all. So the map shows the actin-linked basal route because that is the route these sources establish in this tissue. Whether the basal surface of a colonic cell also carries a second, keratin-linked attachment is a real question that this lesson does not answer, and the gap is left visible instead of being filled with a plausible guess.

scenes.title: Breaking one anchor
scenes.contentHtml:
Breaking one anchor

A tidy diagram invites a tidy error. Four attachments, drawn as one stack, joined to a shared cytoskeleton, all serving the integrity of the sheet. From there it is a short step to a prediction that feels obvious and is wrong.

Misconception
id misconception-one-system

The incorrect model. The junctional complex is one integrated system. Break any structural member of it and the sheet degrades across the board: adhesion weakens, the barrier leaks, the cytoskeleton disorganises, the cells suffer.

Why it is tempting. It is how most built structures behave, and the parts genuinely are adjacent, interdependent in places, and often described together. The phrase "junctional complex" does real damage here by suggesting a single machine.

What actually happens. Delete the desmosome's link to keratin and almost nothing on that list occurs. One specific thing fails, and it is not on the list at all.

The discriminating test. Remove one anchor and check every function separately instead of checking the sheet as a whole. The experiment below does exactly that.

The experiment

Desmoplakin is the cytolinker from the previous scene: the protein that ties keratin filaments to the desmosome. Delete it and the desmosome loses its grip on keratin while everything else about the junction is left in place. That is an unusually clean cut, and it was made.

Investigation
id investigation-desmoplakin-deletion

Setup. Desmoplakin was conditionally deleted in the intestinal epithelium of mice, using a Villin-driven Cre to restrict the deletion to that tissue. Wild-type littermates served as controls.

What failed. Microvilli. They were significantly shortened, and they were often irregularly shaped and vesiculated.

What did not fail. Nearly everything else that was checked.

  • Adherens junctions were intact: E-cadherin localisation was unchanged.
  • Tight junctions were intact: ZO-1 localisation was unchanged. The authors report no changes in the apical junctional complex.
  • The barrier held. A biotin tracer applied to the tissue did not leak along the lateral membranes, and the authors state that desmoplakin is not required for barrier function of the intestinal epithelium.
  • Keratin organisation was indistinguishable from wild type at the light-microscope level, and keratin stayed enriched in the apical region.
  • Desmosomes themselves were still present, in their proper subapical location at each cell-to-cell junction. What they had lost was the attachment of keratin filaments to them.
  • The other desmosomal proteins localised normally: plakoglobin and plakophilin 2 were unaffected.
  • Microtubules were still arranged along the apicobasal axis.
  • Every terminal web component examined was localised as in wild type, at comparable expression levels.

The animals. Indistinguishable from wild-type littermates. Viable, fertile, normal lifespan, normal growth rate, body weight and intestine length. No sign of the inflammation or bacterial infection that a compromised barrier would produce.

The authors' reading. They propose that losing keratin's anchorage to the desmosome weakens the terminal web, so that it can no longer sustain long microvilli, which exert force on the terminal web as they grow out. They offer a second possible route as well, that desmoplakin influences signalling to the actin cytoskeleton, and note the resemblance of the affected microvilli to calcium-treated brush borders, which would implicate villin's severing activity. They say this requires further investigation.

Stated limits. The authors cannot rule out that other proteins partially rescue keratin attachment to the desmosome, which would mean the cut was less clean than intended. The mechanism of apical keratin localisation remains incompletely understood. A worsening of the phenotype in older outbred mice was noticed and not pursued.

What the result licenses, and what it does not

The honest summary is narrow. Removing the keratin anchor removed a keratin-dependent function and left the functions that depend on other anchors alone.

Notice how well that fits the previous scene's map. Adhesion between these cells runs through E-cadherin and catenins to actin, and the seal runs through claudins and ZO proteins to actin. Neither route passes through desmoplakin or keratin, so neither route broke. The map predicted which functions were at risk, and the experiment agrees.

The failure that did occur travelled by an unexpected path, and this is the part worth remembering. Microvillus length is an apical, actin-based property, three scenes' worth of argument away from a lateral desmosome. The connection is the terminal web: keratin anchored at the desmosome contributes to the mat that the actin core bundles are planted in, and a growing microvillus pushes against that mat. Weaken the mat and the projection it supports cannot be held as long. Scene 1's structure and scene 4's structure are mechanically continuous, which no diagram of separate junctions would suggest.

Two cautions on how far this goes.

The proposed route from lost keratin anchorage to shortened microvilli is the authors' interpretation, offered alongside an alternative involving actin signalling, and they call for further work. Treat it as the best current reading of their own result and not as an established mechanism.

And this is mouse small intestine with a tissue-restricted deletion, in animals that were otherwise healthy for a normal lifespan. It shows what one anchor is load-bearing for under ordinary conditions. It does not show what happens to a colonic sheet under mechanical stress, which is the condition where a tension-bearing anchor would be expected to matter most, and which the experiment did not impose.

scenes.title: What moves a cell up a crypt
scenes.contentHtml:
What moves a cell up a crypt

Everything so far has been about holding still: a projection held out, a sheet held together, a cell held onto its mat. The crypt does not hold still. Cells are made at the base, they travel to the surface, and they are shed there, and the whole lining turns over in a few days.

So what moves them?

The textbook answer is that division below pushes them up. It is a good answer, it has real evidence behind it, and it is not settled. This scene is about how to hold a question like that properly, because a learner who files it as settled will be wrong in a way that is hard to undo.

First, get the scale of the movement

Take the migration velocity measured on mouse small-intestinal villi under control conditions: 9.00 ± 0.465 µm per hour in the duodenum, 5.96 ± 0.379 µm per hour in the ileum.

Convert the faster figure into something you can picture. In a day:

9.00 μm/h×24 h=216 μm9.00\ \mu\text{m/h} \times 24\ \text{h} = 216\ \mu\text{m}

And in cells, using this block's working height of about 22 µm for an absorptive cell:

216 μm÷22 μm≈10216\ \mu\text{m} \div 22\ \mu\text{m} \approx 10

Roughly ten cell-lengths a day. A cell in this tissue is displaced by about its own height every two and a half hours, continuously, for the few days it lives. Whatever mechanism does this is not a rare event; it is a steady process running the whole time the sheet is doing its other work.

Position one: the push from below

Cell proliferation in the crypt is the primary force driving migration. The strongest version of this case measured cell positions over time along mouse duodenum and ileum in living animals, together with crypt proliferation rates, across several conditions including a transgenic line in which proliferation was suppressed. Migration velocities on the villi tracked crypt proliferation rates in every condition tested. The authors' conclusion is that proliferation within the crypt is the primary force that drives migration along the villus.

That is a serious result in intact tissue with normal geometry, which is the hardest place to measure anything.

Now read the design carefully. What was measured was a coupling between two rates: how fast cells are produced below, and how fast cells move above. A coupling of that kind is consistent with proliferation pushing cells upward. It is also consistent with proliferation and migration both being set by something further upstream, with neither causing the other. The measurement cannot separate those, because it never measured a force.

The authors are explicit about the residue. They state that they cannot rule out additional mechanisms, naming active migration and villus contraction and expansion, affecting the tight coupling in some cases. They also note a mismatch that their own model does not explain: migration on the villus follows a circadian rhythm, and crypt proliferation does not. A rhythm in the output that is missing from the proposed cause is a real problem for the proposed cause.

Position two: the pull from above

A different study went after the force itself.

Working with mouse intestinal organoids grown on soft gels, it measured traction and monolayer tension directly. The transit amplifying zone came out under tension. Cells were pulled out of the crypt along a gradient of increasing tension, dragged by cells further into the villus-like domain, in the way the trailing edge of a migrating cell cluster is dragged by its leading edge. Cell velocity ran parallel to cell-substrate traction, which is the signature of collective migration and not of being shoved. Blocking myosin II abolished the traction forces and the tissue flattened, so the forces were actomyosin-generated.

These authors put the disagreement in plain terms: the widely assumed mechanism, a pushing force arising from compression downstream of mitotic pressure, is incompatible with their observation that the transit amplifying zone is under tension. Compression and tension have opposite signs. A region cannot be both.

And this design has the complementary weakness. It measured the disputed quantity directly, which the first design could not, but in a preparation the authors themselves qualify: the transit amplifying zone is shorter than in living tissue, the villus geometry is not reproduced, and the cells in the villus-like domain are thinner than in vivo and lack a well-developed brush border.

That last limitation deserves a moment, because this lesson has spent five scenes on the brush border and the terminal web anchored beneath it. A preparation whose cells have not built a proper brush border is missing an apical actin structure that is mechanically continuous with the junctions carrying these very forces. It does not make the force measurement wrong. It does mean the mechanical state of a cell in that dish differs from the mechanical state of a cell in a crypt in a way directly relevant to what was measured.

Holding the question honestly

Lay the two side by side and the shape of the disagreement is clear.

Push from below Pull from above
What was measured positions and proliferation rates over time traction and monolayer tension
Where intact mouse duodenum and ileum, in vivo mouse organoid flattened on a gel
Strength normal tissue, normal geometry measures the force in dispute
Weakness infers the force from a correlation geometry and brush border not reproduced

Neither study is careless and neither is decisive. They differ in what they measured and in the preparation they measured it in, and each is strong exactly where the other is weak. The defensible position is that proliferation in the crypt is tightly coupled to migration and is very likely a major contributor, that actomyosin-generated tension in the sheet is measurably present and pulls cells out of the crypt, and that the relative contribution of the two is open.

What would settle it is not a third opinion. It is a direct measurement of tension or traction in intact tissue with normal three-dimensional geometry, which is the one combination neither study achieved. Until then the circadian mismatch remains the sharpest single piece of evidence against pushing being the whole story, because it is a prediction failure and not a difference of preparation.

A word about the word "motility"

Motility usually calls up a single cell crawling across a dish: a fibroblast extending a free front edge, gripping, and hauling itself forward. Almost none of that describes what happens here, and this lesson has deliberately used no single-cell crawling evidence at all.

An enterocyte never leaves the sheet. It stays joined to its neighbours by every attachment in the previous scene for the whole journey, and it is shed only at the end of it. There is no free leading edge, and the cell in front of it is not empty space but another cell it is bolted to. The organoid study's own description is of collective movement in which a cell's velocity aligns with traction and cells are dragged by those ahead.

Some of the machinery is genuinely shared, and that is the part worth carrying across: actomyosin generates the force in both cases, and integrin-based adhesion to the matrix transmits it in both cases. What does not carry across is the free front edge, the freedom to make and break adhesions at will, and the independence of one cell's direction from its neighbours'. A model of crawling imported wholesale into a crypt predicts a cell that could turn around and leave, and this cell cannot.

scenes.title: Practice: decide, then defend the decision
scenes.contentHtml:
Practice: decide, then defend the decision

Three tasks, with the scaffolding removed as you go. Work each one before reading the discussion under it. The discussion is written to diagnose a wrong route, so read it even when your answer was right.

Task 1, with the steps supplied

A cell in a different tissue needs to hold a straight projection 4 µm long, and it will not be cross-linked into a bundle.

Work through it in this order. First, write down the persistence length of each of the three filament types. Second, compute the ratio of each persistence length to 4 µm. Third, apply the rule that a ratio comfortably above 1 means rod-like over that distance. Fourth, name any candidate that is not excluded, and say what other property you would check next.

Discussion. A single actin filament gives ratios from 3/4 to 17/4, so 0.75 to 4.25. That range straddles 1, which is the interesting answer: at the low end of the published range a single actin filament will not hold 4 µm straight, and at the high end it will. The correct response is that actin is marginal here and the answer depends on where in its range this filament sits, which is exactly why the microvillus case at 1 µm was safe and this one is not. An intermediate filament gives 0.05 to 0.25 and is excluded. A microtubule gives more than 250 and is comfortably sufficient.

If you answered "actin, because actin holds microvilli up", you transferred a conclusion instead of the method. The projection is four times longer, and that changes the arithmetic. The stated condition that it is not bundled is the reason the single-filament figure is the right one to use.

Task 2, with less help

A mutation removes desmoplakin's ability to bind intermediate filaments but leaves the rest of the desmosome assembled and correctly positioned.

Predict what happens to each of the following, and give the anchor your prediction runs through: the seal against material moving between cells; adhesion between neighbouring cells; the length of the microvilli.

Discussion. The seal survives, because it runs from claudins and occludin through ZO proteins to actin, and no part of that route passes through desmoplakin. Adhesion survives, because it runs from E-cadherin and nectin through catenins to actin, again not through desmoplakin. Microvilli shorten, and that is the one that fails, because keratin anchored at the desmosome contributes to the terminal web in which the microvillar actin bundles are planted.

Two errors are worth naming. Predicting that everything degrades treats the complex as one machine and ignores which anchor carries which function. Predicting that only lateral, desmosome-adjacent things fail misses the apical consequence entirely, which is the genuinely surprising part of the real experiment.

Task 3, unscaffolded

An investigator reports that in a mouse line with reduced crypt proliferation, cells on the villus move more slowly, and concludes that mitotic pressure from the crypt is the force that drives migration.

Evaluate the conclusion. State precisely what the observation supports, what it does not support, what alternative explanation survives it, and what single additional measurement would do most to distinguish them.

Discussion. The observation supports a coupling between proliferation rate and migration velocity, and it is real. It does not support the claim that mitotic pressure is the force, because no force was measured. At least two alternatives survive: that a common upstream regulator sets both rates, and that proliferation contributes alongside actomyosin-generated tension in the sheet. The direct traction and tension measurements in organoids found the transit amplifying zone under tension rather than compression, which is the opposite sign to the proposed pushing mechanism.

The measurement that would do most is a direct measurement of tension or traction in intact tissue with normal three-dimensional geometry. Answering "repeat it in more mice" mistakes precision for validity: repeating a correlational design more times yields a better-estimated correlation and no information about the force.

Anyone who wrote that the investigator is simply wrong has overcorrected. The coupling is well measured and probably matters. What is unwarranted is the leap from a coupling to a named mechanical cause.

Accessibility and alternatives

Every number and relationship in this lesson is available in prose, and no task requires seeing a picture.

The junction diagram in scene 4 has a long description stating the same nodes, the same links and the same conclusion, and the argument in that scene is complete without it: the four attachments are named in apical-to-basal order in the text, each with the polymer it anchors. If the diagram does not render or is not visible to you, read the ordered list in the section headed "Down the side of the cell, in order", which carries the same content.

The comparison table in scene 2 and the two-column table in scene 6 are both restated as sentences in the surrounding paragraphs. The stiffness ratio is given as a named relation in words as well as symbols: divide the filament's persistence length by the length of the structure, and compare the answer with 1. Each calculation in scene 3 is written out in full as a division with its result, so no step depends on reading a symbolic form.

The arithmetic throughout uses division and comparison to 1. A calculator is fine and no mental arithmetic is required or timed. There is no drag interaction, no audio carrying unique information, and no colour-coded distinction anywhere in the pack.

Nothing in this lesson asks you for your own physiology, symptoms, medication or medical history, and no task requires observing your own body.

Recovery route

If the arithmetic in scene 3 did not land, the problem is usually the ratio and not the biology. Return to PREM-QNT-003 on ratios and proportions, then re-run just Demand 1 and Demand 2 of the worked example, which differ only in the length you divide by.

If the three filament systems keep blurring together, stop trying to hold three names and hold two numbers instead: a persistence length of about 10 µm for actin and more than 1 mm for microtubules. Then attach the third by its opposite, since intermediate filaments are the floppy, motorless, unbreakable one. Names attached to a property are recoverable; names attached to other names are not.

If the junction hierarchy will not stay in order, learn the sealing fact first. Only the tight junction closes the space between cells, and it is the topmost of the three. The other two hold cells together without sealing. Once that is fixed, add the polymer: the desmosome is the odd one out, and it grips keratin.

If scene 6 felt unsatisfying because it did not resolve, that reaction is the right one to examine rather than to fix. PREM-SCI-007 on correlation, causation and confounding and PREM-SCI-011 on mechanistic and convergent evidence both bear directly on it. A question that two good studies answer differently is a question with a live disagreement in it, and reporting it as decided would be the error.

If a task went wrong, the fastest diagnosis is to ask which property you compared. Most wrong answers in this material come from comparing stiffness when the demand named deformation, or from comparing anything at all when the demand named direction.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: which attachment does a leak implicate?
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: which attachment does a leak implicate?

Callout

This case is a teaching example, not medical advice. It carries no diagnosis, no dose, no regimen and no recommendation, and nothing in it should be used to interpret a real person's results. Its purpose is to show what this lesson's model does and does not license a reader to conclude.

Here is a question a clinician actually faces. A colonic epithelium is behaving as though material is crossing it that should not be. Something in the lining has given way. Which of the four attachments does that finding point at, and how confidently?

The lesson answers the first half sharply and the second half with care.

The reasoning the model supports

Of the three cell-to-cell attachments, only the tight junction seals the space between neighbouring cells. At the tight junction the intercellular space disappears entirely. At the adherens junction and the desmosome the neighbouring membranes stay 15 to 20 nanometres apart, and both of those attachments hold cells together without closing the gap. The tight junction is the rate-limiting step for anything travelling between cells instead of through them.

So a leak along the route between cells points at the tight junction, and specifically at its claudins, occludin and JAM-A and the ZO scaffolds tying them to actin. It does not point at adhesion in general, because adhesion and sealing are different jobs done by different structures.

That is a prediction, and this lesson has already seen it tested from the other direction. In the desmoplakin experiment the desmosome lost its keratin anchor, adhesion between cells was left intact, and the barrier held: a biotin tracer did not leak along the lateral membranes, and the authors state that desmoplakin is not required for the barrier function of the intestinal epithelium. Breaking a non-sealing attachment did not produce a leak. The division of labour is real, and it survived a direct test.

What the clinical literature adds, and how firmly

Changes in tight junction proteins are reported in several intestinal conditions. Decreased expression and redistribution of claudins 3, 5 and 8 have been described in the intestine of people with Crohn's disease; decreased expression and redistribution of claudins 1 and 4 in ulcerative colitis; decreased ZO-1 in coeliac disease; and decreased claudin 1 in small-intestinal biopsy specimens from people with food allergy after exposure to the relevant allergen.

Read the verbs. Described, reported, observed. These are associations between a disease state and a protein finding, and the review reporting them does not establish whether the junction change causes the disease or results from it. That distinction is not a technicality. If the junction change is a consequence of inflammation, then targeting the junction treats a symptom; if it is a cause, the same intervention treats the disease. The same association supports both stories.

This is the discipline PREM-SCI-007 set out, arriving in a place where it has consequences. The lesson's structural model tells you which component a leak implicates. It does not tell you the direction of causation in a disease, and no amount of confidence about claudins supplies it.

Working the case

Worked Example
id worked-example-barrier-reasoning

The finding. In a research setting, colonic tissue from a person with active colitis shows reduced claudin expression and increased movement of a tracer between cells, compared with tissue from people without colitis.

Step 1: which structure does the model implicate? The tight junction. It is the only one of the three cell-to-cell attachments that closes the space between cells, and claudins are among its transmembrane proteins. The finding and the model agree.

Step 2: what is the mechanism of the leak, in structural terms? Reduced claudin means fewer of the proteins that form the selective pores and seal the space. A paracellular route that was closed is less closed. This part is a structural inference from the composition of the junction and is well supported.

Step 3: what caused the claudin reduction? Unknown from this finding. Inflammation in colitis could reduce claudin expression, or reduced claudin could permit luminal material through and drive inflammation, or a third factor could produce both. The finding is a snapshot of two things that co-occur.

Step 4: what would distinguish them? Something that establishes order or intervention. A measurement showing the junction change preceding the inflammation, or an intervention that alters only the junction and then changes disease activity. Neither is supplied by an association in tissue sampled once.

Step 5: what may be concluded? That the barrier defect is located at the tight junction rather than at the adhesive attachments, which is genuinely useful and follows from the structural model. Not that fixing claudins would treat the colitis.

Step 6: what the model rules out. A hypothesis that the leak arises from failed desmosomal adhesion is a poor fit, because desmosomes do not seal the paracellular space and because removing the desmosome's keratin anchor left the barrier intact. This is the lesson's own map doing diagnostic work: knowing which polymer anchors which junction tells you which explanations to stop considering.

Where the block goes next

Three questions lesson 04 handed forward have now been answered. A microvillus is held up by a bundle of about nineteen actin filaments, guyed to its membrane by myosin cross-bridges and planted in a spectrin-containing terminal web. A junction is a specific set of proteins reaching across to a neighbour and gripping a specific polymer on the inside. And the sealing job, the adhesive job and the load-bearing job belong to different attachments, which is why they fail separately.

One question has been answered honestly rather than fully. What drives the climb is still contested, and the lesson said so.

Lesson 08 takes up the division at the crypt base that supplies every cell making this journey, which is where the proliferation half of that argument gets its machinery. Lesson 10 returns to the end of the journey, where cells are shed, and to what happens when the climb stops ending.

items.prompt: A cell must hold a straight projection 2 micrometres long, and the actin filament inside it is a single filament that is not cross-linked into a bundle. Taking 10 micrometres as the working persistence length of a single actin filament, compute the ratio of persistence length to the length that must be held straight. Give the ratio as a number.

answer.reasoning: The ratio is the persistence length divided by the length of the structure: 10 micrometres divided by 2 micrometres gives 5. Because 5 is comfortably greater than 1, a single actin filament stays essentially straight over 2 micrometres and can hold the projection on its own. Both numbers the calculation needs are supplied in the stem, and the stem states that the filament is not bundled, which is why the single-filament figure is the correct one to use rather than a bundle's higher effective stiffness.
commonErrors: Inverting the ratio to give 0.2, which divides the structure length by the persistence length and reverses the interpretation.
Using the height of a cell instead of the 2 micrometres given in the stem.
Answering with a filament name instead of the number the item asks for.

items.prompt: A cell needs to carry a vesicle from the Golgi to one particular face of the cell, a distance of 18 micrometres. Which statement correctly names the filament system suited to the task and the property that decides it? Use the persistence lengths given in this lesson: 3 to 17 micrometres for a single actin filament, greater than 1 millimetre for a microtubule, and a few hundred nanometres to about 1 micrometre for an intermediate filament.

options.text: Intermediate filaments, because they are the most extensible of the three and can stretch to reach the destination.
Microtubules, because they are polar and carry kinesins and dyneins, so a particular destination can be selected, and they are stiff over this distance.
Actin filaments, because a single actin filament's persistence length exceeds 18 micrometres.
Any of the three, because all three form networks that span the whole cell.
Intermediate filaments, because being apolar means they are not restricted to one direction and can deliver to any face.

answer.reasoning: The demand names a particular destination, so the deciding property is direction. Only a polar filament has ends that differ, and only a polar filament carries motors that can tell those ends apart; microtubules are polar and carry kinesins and dyneins. Their persistence length of more than 1 millimetre also makes them rod-like across 18 micrometres, so stiffness agrees with polarity here. The actin option is false on the arithmetic supplied: the published range tops out at 17 micrometres, which is less than 18, so a single actin filament's persistence length does not exceed the distance. Both intermediate filament options are false because intermediate filaments carry no molecular motors at all, and apolarity is what prevents directed delivery rather than what enables it.
commonErrors: Reading apolarity as freedom of direction when it means no direction can be selected.
Treating extensibility as relevant to a transport demand.
Assuming actin transfers from the microvillus case without rechecking the ratio over the longer distance.

The adherens junction is linked to actin through catenins.
The desmosome is linked to keratin intermediate filaments through desmoplakin.
The desmosome is linked to actin through catenins.
The adherens junction is linked to keratin intermediate filaments through desmoplakin.
Basal integrins are linked to actin through integrin-linked kinase.

answer.summary: All four actin and keratin pairings are correct; the two that swap the desmosome and adherens junction are not.

items.prompt: A study measures cell positions over time in mouse small intestine and finds that when crypt proliferation is suppressed, migration velocity along the villus falls. The authors conclude that mitotic pressure from the crypt is the force that drives migration. Which is the strongest objection to that conclusion as stated?

options.text: No force was measured, so the coupling between the two rates is equally consistent with proliferation and migration both being set by a common upstream factor.
Migration velocities cannot be measured accurately in living mice, so the observation is unreliable.
Proliferation has no effect on migration, so the observed relationship must be an artefact.
The study needed more animals, because a larger sample would have established the mechanism.
Direct tension measurements in organoids proved that proliferation makes no contribution to migration.

answer.summary: The design measured a correlation between two rates, not a force.
answer.reasoning: The observation is a coupling between how fast cells are produced and how fast they move. That is consistent with proliferation pushing cells upward, and equally consistent with a common upstream regulator setting both rates, and the design cannot separate the two because it never measured a force. The remaining options each fail for a different reason. The velocities were measured, and the authors of this work report them with confidence intervals, so unreliability is not the objection. Denying any effect contradicts the coupling actually observed and also overstates the case in the opposite direction. Adding animals improves the precision of a correlation and yields no information about a force, so it mistakes precision for validity. And the organoid work found the transit amplifying zone under tension, which contradicts a purely compressive pushing mechanism; it did not show that proliferation contributes nothing, and claiming it did would overstate that study as badly as the original conclusion overstates its own.
commonErrors: Overcorrecting to the claim that proliferation is irrelevant, which the evidence does not support.
Treating a larger sample as a remedy for a design that cannot measure the quantity in dispute.
Reading the organoid tension result as a refutation of any proliferative contribution rather than of a purely compressive mechanism.

items.prompt:
Two studies disagree about what moves cells up a crypt. One measured cell positions and crypt proliferation rates over time in intact mouse duodenum and ileum, and concluded that crypt proliferation is the primary force driving migration. The other measured traction and monolayer tension directly in mouse intestinal organoids grown on soft gels, found the transit amplifying zone to be under tension, and stated that a pushing force from compression downstream of mitotic pressure is incompatible with that observation.

In no more than 300 words: state what each design can establish about the driving force and what it cannot; explain why the two results are not simply reconcilable as a matter of degree; name one limitation each study's own authors report; and name the single measurement that would do most to discriminate between the accounts.

answer.correct:
Each design answers a different question. The in vivo work establishes a real coupling: suppress crypt proliferation and villus migration velocity falls, measured in normal tissue with normal geometry. What it cannot establish is a force, because it never measured one. A coupling between two rates is equally consistent with proliferation pushing cells upward and with a common upstream regulator setting both rates, and this design cannot separate those. The organoid work measured the disputed quantity directly, by monolayer stress microscopy, which the first design could not do at all. What it cannot establish is that the same holds in vivo, because the preparation is altered.

The two results are not a matter of degree because they assign opposite signs to the same region. A pushing mechanism requires the transit amplifying zone to be under compression; the measurement found it under tension. A region cannot be both, so this is not a question of how much each contributes but of which description of that zone is right.

Each set of authors names its own limits. The in vivo authors say they cannot rule out additional mechanisms such as active migration or villus contraction and expansion, and they report a circadian rhythm in villus migration that crypt proliferation does not show. The organoid authors say their transit amplifying zone is shorter than in vivo, that villus geometry is not recapitulated, and that their villus-domain cells are thinner and lack a well-developed brush border.

The discriminating measurement is a direct measurement of tension or traction in intact tissue with normal three-dimensional geometry. That is the one combination neither study achieved, and it is the measurement that would decide the sign of the stress in the transit amplifying zone. Until it exists, the defensible position is that proliferation is tightly coupled to migration and probably contributes, that actomyosin-generated tension is measurably present, and that the relative contribution is open.
answer.summary: The in vivo study establishes a coupling but not a force; the organoid study measures the force but in an altered geometry; compression and tension have opposite signs; and the discriminating measurement is direct tension or traction in intact three-dimensional tissue.
answer.reasoning: A full response makes four moves. First, what each design shows: the in vivo work establishes a real coupling between crypt proliferation rate and villus migration velocity in normal tissue with normal geometry, but it inferred the force from that correlation and never measured one, so it cannot exclude a common upstream regulator setting both rates. The organoid work measured the disputed quantity directly by monolayer stress microscopy, which the first design could not do, but in an altered preparation. Second, why this is not a matter of degree: the two accounts assign opposite signs to the same region. A pushing mechanism requires the transit amplifying zone to be under compression, and the measurement found it under tension, and a region cannot be both at once. Third, the authors' own limitations: the in vivo authors state they cannot rule out additional mechanisms such as active migration or villus contraction and expansion, and they report a circadian rhythm in villus migration that crypt proliferation does not show; the organoid authors state that their transit amplifying zone is shorter than in vivo, that villus geometry is not recapitulated, and that villus-domain cells are thinner than in vivo and lack a well-developed brush border. Fourth, the discriminating measurement: a direct measurement of tension or traction in intact tissue with normal three-dimensional geometry, which is the one combination neither study achieved. A strong response also notes that the defensible current position is that proliferation is tightly coupled to migration and probably contributes, that actomyosin-generated tension is measurably present, and that the relative contribution is open.
acceptableResponses: Any response that distinguishes a measured correlation from a measured force, identifies the opposite signs of compression and tension as the reason the disagreement is not one of degree, reports at least one author-stated limitation from each study accurately, and names a direct force or tension measurement in intact three-dimensional tissue as the discriminating step.
commonErrors: Concluding that one study is simply right and the other wrong, when each is strong where the other is weak.
Treating the disagreement as a difference of magnitude, which misses that compression and tension have opposite signs.
Inventing a limitation instead of reporting one the authors state.
Proposing replication or a larger sample as the discriminating measurement.
Asserting that the question is settled in either direction.
